# Supporting Human-AI Teams:Transparency, explainability, and situation awareness

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Mica R. Endsley \*

SA Technologies, USA

A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords: Situation awareness Transparency Explainable AI Human-AI teams Tesla

## A B S T R A C T

System autonomy and AI are being developed for a wide variety of applications where they will likely work in tandem with people, forming human-AI teams (HAT). Situation awareness (SA) of autonomous systems and AI has been established as critical for effective interaction and oversight of these systems. As AI capabilities grow, and more effective teaming behaviors are expected of AI systems, there will also be an increased need for shared SA between the human and AI teammates. Methods for supporting team SA within HAT are discussed in terms of team SA requirements, team SA mechanisms, team SA displays and team SA processes. A framework for understanding the types of information that needs to be shared within HAT is provided, including a focus on taskwork SA, agent SA, and teamwork SA. AI based on learning systems creates new challenges for the development of good SA and mental models. AI transparency and explainability are discussed in terms of their separate roles for supporting SA and mental models in HAT. The SA Oriented Design (SAOD) process is described as a systematic methodology for developing transparent AI displays for HAT and an example of its application to automated driving in a Tesla is provided.

## 1. Introduction

Autonomous systems are being developed for a wide variety of applications, including driving, aviation, search and rescue, military command and control, space exploration, and many industrial processes. While traditional forms of automation have focused on performing tasks for people, autonomous systems use “intelligence-based capabilities that can respond to situations that were not explicitly programmed or were not anticipated in the design of the technology.” (U.S. Air Force, 2013). Generally empowered through artificial intelligence (AI) software, these systems purport to provide vastly increased capabilities for performing complex tasks (Konaev, Chahal, Fedasiuk, Huang, & Rahkovsky, 2020; Kunze, Hawes, Duckett, Hanheide, & Krajník, 2018).

Even though AI software continues to improve over time, a number of key challenges exist that may cause it remain insufficiently reliable and robust to act alone in safety critical settings, however, including:

1) Perceptual limitations that undermine its performance (Akhtar & Mian, 2018; Alcorn et al., 2019);

2) Hidden biases that lead to inaccurate results by inappropriately overgeneralizing limited training data to broader classes of situations (Ferrer, van Nuenen, Such, Coté, & Criado, 2021; Howard & Borenstein, 2018);

3) The lack a model of causation which is important for supporting advanced functions, such as projections of evolving situations, that are needed for decision making (Littman et al., 2021; Pearl & Mackenzie, 2018); and

4) Brittleness when encountering new types of situations, as even AI that is capable of learning requires repeated exposures to tease out new classes of situations (i.e., they are data hungry) resulting in a learning lag.

It is therefore expected that, for the foreseeable future, AI will need to act in concert with people in order to achieve the desired and necessary performance outcomes. In other words, rather than fully autonomous systems, it is anticipated that semi-autonomous systems, acting in concert with people, will be prevalent.

Developing effective ways of combining humans and system autonomy is therefore receiving considerable attention (Boardman & Butcher, 2019; Endsley, 2017b; Lyons, Sycara, Lewis, & Capiola, 2021; McNeese, Demir, Cooke, & Myers, 2018; National Academies of Sciences Engi neering and Medicine, 2021; O’Neill, McNeese, Barron, & Schelble, 2020; Shively et al., 2017; U. S. Air Force, 2015). Shneiderman (2022) advocates for human-centered AI which emphasizes the importance of designing the AI to work in manner that supports human cognition and performance needs. This view emphasizes the importance of empowering people and enhancing human performance as key goals of AI design due to the fact that humans are ultimately responsible for outcomes (both legally and morally), and because humans have characteristics, such as creativity, empathy and intuition, that should be supported. In addition, people function more effectively when their level of engagement is high (Endsley & Kiris, 1995) which indicates the need to keep people active in their role on the team. As a practical matter, the development of human-centered AI is a basic imperative for developing AI systems that will perform acceptably in many domains.

Others have discussed developing human-autonomy teams (HAT) (Endsley, 2017a; Johnson & Vera, 2019; National Academies of Sciences Engineering and Medicine, 2021; O’Neill et al., 2020; Shively et al., 2017; U. S. Air Force, 2015). The ultimate goal of such collaboration is improved coordination of joint and related tasks, an improved ability to provide mutual support and back-up in the face of unexpected events, and the ability to rapidly adapt to changing demands (National Academies of Sciences Engineering and Medicine, 2021). As AI systems increase in their ability to perform highly cognitive tasks, it is anticipated that these behaviors will become even more important (Johnson, Vignatti, & Duran, 2020). By considering the role of the AI system within the broader context of its operations, and the tasks and activities of the people who must work with it, the overall resilience of the HAT is optimized. In this view, support for HAT functionality is critical for achieving the objectives of human-centered AI.

Many questions regarding how to achieve an effective HAT arise however (National Academies of Sciences Engineering and Medicine, 2021; O’Neill et al., 2020). The form of the HAT could vary, for example, based on a consideration of who is in charge and how interrelated the tasks of the human and autonomy. Different concepts of operation (COOs) could potentially include: a) humans acting as a supervisor over AI that acts as an aid or an assistant, b) humans and AI acting as collaborating teammates, or c) AI that oversees and acts as a limit on human performance (Endsley, 2017b). Other roles for AI systems might include coach, trainer or facilitator. Although a great deal of previous research has focused on the supervisory control COO, new research is also exploring more collaborative paradigms.

Cuevas, Fiore, Caldwell, and Strater (2007, p. B64) define a HAT as “the dynamic, interdependent coupling between one or more human operators and one or more automated systems requiring collaboration and coordination to achieve successful task completion.” They emphasize the importance of a two-way flow of information and a wide range of team-like behaviors, such as collaboration, coordination, and support for joint planning and replanning; reprioritization of goals; and reallocation of tasks. A number of key capabilities for intelligent systems working in teams have been identified, including the ability to (a) enter into a basic compact of joint goals and understood roles, and signal the other team members when they cannot perform their assigned tasks; (b) possess adequate mental models of each other; (c) be predictable to each other; (d) be directable; (e) share their status and intentions; (f) be able to interpret the status and intentions of the other team members; (g) be able to negotiate goals, particularly when situations change and adaptations are necessary; (h) collaborate to include problem solving, replanning, and retasking as needed; (i) redirect teammates’ attention to important signals, activities, and changes without overwhelming each other; and (j) manage the costs of coordination to maintain acceptable workload levels (Klein, Woods, Bradshaw, Hoffman, & Feltovich, 2004).

A number of key factors affecting the successful performance of HATs have been identified as shown in Fig. 1 that require new research advances (National Academies of Sciences Engineering and Medicine, 2021). This includes the need to design AI systems to avoid introducing decision biases, fostering appropriate levels of trust, creating effective team processes and communication strategies, and the need to support team situation awareness (SA) within HAT.

Team SA is critical to effective HAT performance in that it affects the key processes of decision making, teamwork, coordination, and trust. First, overseeing the performance of the autonomous system and developing timely and appropriate interventions requires good SA. Further, the broader range of team behaviors (such as collaboration, coordination, joint planning and replanning, reprioritization of goals, and reallocation of tasks) also rely significantly on the individual’s SA regarding the state of the system and the autonomy. When viewed from the standpoint of the system autonomy, similarly, SA is critical for making appropriate decisions, as well as for understanding what tasks the human teammate is performing (or not performing), and how well they are doing, allowing it to provide appropriate types of back up and support, and for determining human goals and priorities so as to better align tasks and functions across the HAT.

In addition, SA is critical for developing appropriate levels of trust in HATs. While general trust in autonomy may be formed over time based on a number of factors, it is also highly situational in nature (Hoff & Bashir, 2015; U. S. Air Force, 2015). That is, people need to know how capable the system is or is not for performing its tasks under the current conditions (i.e., situational trust). Good SA is therefore essential to accurately calibrated trust in HATs. For a review of factors affecting trust in HATs, see Hoff and Bashir (2015), Schaefer, et al. (2016), Kaplan, et al. (2021), Glikson and Woolley (2020), and Chiou and Lee (2021).

Due to its centrality for effective HAT performance, the goal of this paper is to better define situation awareness needs for HAT and how to best support good SA in HATs. This effort will build from the extensive research base on SA in both individuals and teams, as well as research on SA of automation and AI systems. While SA has received considerable attention with respect to human oversight of automated systems, and to its role in team performance, its extension to HATs is more fledgling.

I will focus on two popular methods for supporting SA of AI systems transparency and explainability — providing a discussion of their relative benefits and limitations for SA in HAT. Although transparency and explainability of AI have received considerable recent research attention, this work has often not been well connected to SA and the role that such approaches need to play with respect to each other in supporting SA within the HAT. For example, the types of SA information identified as relevant for transparency have been highly inconsistent.

Nor are methods for achieving the goal of AI transparency consistently applied or well understood. Finally, I discuss additional considerations for the role of team processes on SA in HAT and future directions for research in this area.

## 2. Situation awareness in Human-AI teams

## 2.1. SA and human decision making

Situation awareness is defined as “the perception of the elements in the environment within a volume of space and time, the comprehension of their meaning, and the projection of their status in the near future” (Endsley, 1988). As a constantly updated state of knowledge about what is happening in a dynamically changing world, it has often been discussed in terms of three ascending levels of SA (Endsley, 1995, 2015).

(1) Level 1 SA – The perception of key information relevant to the decision maker’s needs, which can include information gathered directly via a person’s senses, or through electronic sensors, reports, communications with others, or other means. Thus, it includes information gathered from natural, engineered and human sources.

(2) Level 2 SA - The comprehension or understanding the significance of that information with regard to the decision makers goals. SA involves knowing more than just data; it also includes being able to put together disparate pieces of data to inform relevant decisions, and interpreting what that data means. Level 2 SA is highly dependent on the goals and decision requirements of the individual based on their role (e.g., pilot vs air traffic controller).

(3) Level 3 SA – Projection of the current situation to inform likely or possible future situations. Projection forms the third and highest level of SA, and is the hallmark of expertise in SA (Endsley, 1995, 2018). By constantly projecting ahead, decision makers are able to act proactively instead of just reactively.

The higher levels of SA, comprehension and projection, allow people to function in a timely and effective manner, even with very complex and challenging tasks. Endsley (1995, 2015) provides a model of SA that includes environmental factors (e.g., workload, complexity, stress) as well as individual and system factors. A person’s SA is the outcome of a number of cognitive processes including attention, working memory, pattern matching to schema, and mental models that aid interpretation and projection of current trends into the future. As such, people’s ability to form SA in complex and dynamic worlds is dependent on both individual capabilities as well as training and experience (Endsley, 2018). In addition, SA is significantly impacted by a number of technology attributes, such as the capability of systems for providing needed information (e.g., sensors, datalink, and communications), the design of the user interface that affects how rapidly and accurately people can keep up with changing information, as well as any automation (Endsley & Jones, 2012).

A recent meta-analysis showed that SA is highly predictive of human performance (Endsley, 2021c). Due to its importance, a significant body of research over the past 30 years has focused on SA in complex systems, with a large body of this work focused on SA with automated systems and AI. See (Endsley, 2021a; Endsley & Jones, 2012) for a review. While most of this work has focused on human SA, it is also being extended to the development of AI systems that must form an accurate understanding of situational context in order to act appropriately (Kokar & Endsley, 2012).

## 2.2. Challenges for human SA within HAT

Maintaining SA of the state of the AI and information relevant to the tasks it is performing is a fundamental requirement for effective oversight of AI (Endsley, 2017b). People must be able to tell whether an AI system is accurately assessing relevant information (or if it is missing critical data due to a malfunctioning sensor or capability limitations, for example). They also need to understand the capabilities and limitations of the AI to know whether it can perform correctly in current or upcoming circumstances, and they need to understand its state or mode. SA directly influences their ability correctly decide when to over-ride the advice or actions of the system. SA of the autonomy will be directly impacted by the person’s mental model of the system, as well as by the design of the autonomy in terms of its interaction paradigm and its interface with the human.

Unfortunately, people have been found to have considerable challenges in maintaining SA when working with automated and autonomous systems. First, people are significantly compromised in their ability to oversee autonomy due to their lowered SA when acting as monitors (Endsley, 2017b; Endsley & Kiris, 1995). They can easily become out-of-the-loop and unable to intervene in a timely or correct manner (Moray, 1986; Wiener & Curry, 1980). This has been found to be due to problems in maintaining vigilance over time, often insufficient information on how the system is performing, and reduced levels of cognitive engagement that occur when people passively, rather than actively, perform tasks (Endsley, 2017b; Endsley & Kiris, 1995). This lowered SA can directly contribute to catastrophic failures (Wickens, 2000). Even when deciding whether to accept AI advice, people’s judgements are directly affected by the reliability of the system (Endsley, Bolte, & Jones, 2003). They are both slower to make a decision and more likely to make errors when the system is wrong (Kibbe & McDowell, 1995; Selcon, 1990; Yeh & Wickens, 2001).

In addition, confusion in understanding what autonomous systems are doing, or will do in future, are common (Sarter & Woods, 1995; Wiener & Curry, 1980). Because AI is based on learning techniques, and will therefore change in its capabilities over time, it is likely that the opportunity for confusion will only be further exacerbated (U. S. Air Force, 2015). Additional challenges, such as workload spikes (Bainbridge, 1983) and degradation of manual skills (Casner, Geven, Recker, & Schooler, 2014; Young, Fanjoy, & Suckow, 2006), also will compromise people’s ability to adequately oversee AI. Policies that require people to monitor AI and correct for its deficiencies are hollow unless people have the ability to do so effectively.

## 2.3. Team SA and shared SA within HAT

In moving from individual performance to the broader construct of a HAT, it also becomes relevant to think of team SA and shared SA within the team. Team SA is defined as “the degree to which every team member has the SA required for his or her responsibilities” (Endsley, 1995, p. 39), and is significantly predictive of team performance across many different settings and tasks (Cooke, Kiekel, & Helm, 2001; Crozier et al., 2015; Gardner, Kosemund, & Martinez, 2017; Parush, Hazan, & Shtekelmacher, 2017; Prince, Ellis, Brannick, & Salas, 2007). For the HAT, this simply means that the AI needs to have correct SA for its assigned functions, and people need to have correct SA for their assigned functions. (In this sense, SA of the AI system is not construed to mean actual awareness or consciousness, but rather an accurate situation model on which its decisions are based.)

Shared SA, a subset of team SA, has been defined as “the degree to which team members possess the same SA on shared SA requirements” (Endsley & Jones, 2001, p. 48), Fig. 2. Because responsibilities in a team only partially overlap, the SA requirements that are in common to any two team members also only partially overlap. Shared SA has also been shown to predict team performance (Bonney, Davis-Sramek, & Cadotte, 2016; Cooke et al., 2001; Coolen, Draaisma, & Loeffen, 2019; Rosenman et al., 2018).

One requirement for effective team performance is that members of a team have the same SA on aspects of the situation that are relevant to their shared goals in order to support coordinated team performance.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 2. Team SA and shared SA (from Endsley & Jones, 2001).

For example, a pilot and air traffic controller do not need to have shared SA of all information, but they do need to have shared SA of the clearance altitude or landing runway assigned to the pilot’s plane, and its current position, heading and altitude. Studies have shown that it is important that shared displays in teams focus on shared SA needs, for example, so as to avoid overload that can occur by sharing all of the information that different teammates may need for other tasks (Bolstad & Endsley, 1999, 2000).

Although team and shared SA have traditionally been considered in relation to teams of people, it also has an important role for supporting performance in HAT. Not only is it important that both the AI and the human have accurate SA for their tasks, and shared (consistent) SA on information relevant to both, but people will need to have accurate SA of the state of the AI and the AI will likely need to form SA on the state of its human teammates. Shared SA in HAT is critical for helping teams to manage shared interdependencies and create goal alignment (National Academies of Sciences Engineering and Medicine, 2021). Successful coordination across interdependent tasks and functions requires sharing this higher-level information on goals, plans and functional assignments that underly dynamic task performance. This includes the ability of the AI to proactively provide relevant, contextually appropriate information and to support accurate levels of confidence and trust (National Academies of Sciences Engineering and Medicine, 2021).

The information that is relevant to team SA for HAT and methods for supporting it will be considered in more depth through the lens of a model of team SA which identities four major components that determine the ability to achieve successful team SA in human-human teams (Endsley, 2021a; Endsley & Jones, 1997, 2001):

a) Team SA Requirements – the information that is needed to support the SA and shared SA of the team as defined in Table 1;

b) Team SA Mechanisms – primarily shared mental models that support the ability of the team to achieve accurate shared SA;

c) Team SA Devices - methods for sharing information across the team, including communications (verbal and non-verbal), a shared environment (allowing direct observation of information), and shared displays; and

d) Team SA Processes – which are important for effective communication and coordination in teams that directly support shared SA.

This model provides a foundation for developing insights into four major components that will be needed to support team SA in HAT, and which will guide the remainder of the discussion.

## 3. Team SA requirements in HAT

The SA requirements for the HAT can be considered along several dimensions, as shown in Fig. 3. From the perspective of the human teammate, SA is needed of the state of the world (e.g., the system being operated and its current environment), and of the AI teammate, as well as SA of oneself (i.e., meta-SA). Similarly, team SA may also be considered from the perspective of the AI, which would need to have SA of the state of the world, and potentially of its human teammate, as well as its own ability to perform tasks. Along these lines, the need for shared SA in HAT is portrayed as a combination of shared SA needs associated with the task domain, along with additional shared SA needs associated with team performance, taken from both the perspective of the human and AI teammates.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 3. Shared SA needs in HAT.

Cannon-Bowers, Salas, and Converse (1993) describe two key aspects of team performance: taskwork and teamwork. This dichotomy can be used to better describe SA needs for HAT, along with some unique properties associated with agent SA, as shown in Table 1. Each of these contributors to shared SA in HAT will be described in more detail.

Table 1

Shared SA requirements in human-AI teams.

| SA Area | Supports | Shared SA Needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Taskwork SA- SA of World and System | Task Performance | Perception (Level 1)Comprehension (Level 2)Projection (Level 3) |
| Agent SA- SA of Teammate and Self | Agent Oversight,Intervention &amp; Backup | State/ModeSA Sufficiency (meta-awareness)Ability to Perform TasksTask Status &amp;PerformanceProjected ActionsImpact of Actions on Others |

## 3.1. Taskwork SA

The SA requirements relevant to the performance of tasks for any given role is typically determined via a goal-directed task analysis (GDTA for each operational role in a system (Endsley, 1993; Endsley, Farley, Jones, Midkiff, & Hansman, 1998; Endsley & Rodgers, 1994; Matthews, Strater, & Endsley, 2004). For example, the pilots of an aircraft have unique SA requirements for their role, and air traffic controllers have different SA requirements to support the decisions that they need to make to achieve their operational goals.

In the GDTA, SA requirements are specified for each goal and decision to include a) the basic data that is needed to support perception (level 1 SA) needs, b) the comprehension or understanding of the data relevant to operator goals that is needed (level 2 SA), and c) the projections or anticipated future states of relevant elements (level 3 SA) that support proactive decision making (Endsley & Jones, 2012). SA requirements can be thought of as the information about the system that is being operated (within the context of the operational tasks and goals to be performed) and the world in which it is operating (including environment and other entities) as needed to support real-time decision making associated with goal attainment.

The GDTA has been extended to teams by providing a mechanism for identifying the specific information that needs to be shared between teammates, i.e., the information that supports a common understanding in relation to the shared goals in a team (Bolstad, Riley, Jones, & Endsley, 2002; Endsley & Jones, 2001). Thus, the relevant task related information associated with the system and its environment can be specifically identified for any teammate, along with the information (at all three levels of SA) that they need to use to form a common picture that is needed for effective team performance.

This methodology can also be extended to determine the task relevant shared SA needs for HAT. The information needed by each teammate can be identified, along with the information that needs to be shared. In the case of HAT involving supervisory control, where the human teammate has responsibility for overseeing the performance of the AI, the human will continue to need SA over all aspects of the task, no matter which entity is assigned responsibility for performing a function (human, AI or a combination). Because people have the requirement to oversee the performance of AI, they also need to have an understanding of the relevant information (at all 3 levels of SA) in order to perform that oversight effectively.

As an example for better understanding SA within a HAT, human-AI interaction in automated vehicles (AV) can serve as an illustration. AVs are emblematic of system autonomy based on AI, and while these systems are not currently exhibiting “team-like” behaviors, it is possible that they could do so in future if they possessed improved levels of SA and were better able to support human SA needs for interacting with them.

In this example, both the AI and a driver overseeing the AI that is making a decision on whether a lane change is needed for an automated vehicle would need to have SA of the elements in Table 2 in order to either make the decision or to determine if the agent making the decision was doing so correctly. (Additional SA requirements are associated with the decision of whether a lane change is safe and legal, also relevant to this goal.)

| Do I need to | Projected | Need for lane change | Distance to next turn |
| change lanes? | lane needed |  | or highway transition Position on route Planned route |

Shared SA needs relevant to common goals are depicted in Fig. 4, which shows that SA should be consistent across the team on these SA requirements because they fall into the responsibilities and goals of both the human and the AI teammate (either for performing or overseeing the relevant goal attainment). When there is a misalignment (people’s understanding of the situation is different than the system’s), there may be a failure to correctly intervene in the system’s actions, or conversely people may incorrectly intervene when it is not appropriate (i.e., undertrust the AI). At a minimum, it will take time for people and AI to reconcile differences that exist. When the human does not have SA of the AI’s situation model (driving its actions and intentions), they will be challenged to effectively perform an oversight role, able to react only once errors occur. Conversely, if AI is overseeing human performance, similar alignments will be needed.

An important element of SA in many domains is the level of confidence or reliability associated with information. How much confidence people have in their perceptions of the data, their assessments of that data and the projections they make from the data are all relevant to their decision making (Endsley, 2020; Endsley & Jones, 1997). Similarly, AI will often have reliability or confidence levels associated with data classifications or projections. This information is a very important part of SA (at all 3 levels) that needs to be conveyed between the human and AI as a component of shared SA.

## 3.2. Agent SA

In addition, across many domains and systems there is a need for people to have SA of how well both they and their teammates are performing (i.e., agent SA). In an effective human-human team, people monitor their teammates to determine if they are overloaded or able to perform properly (e.g., fatigued, experienced on the task), and adjust task assignments accordingly (Endsley et al., 1998; Endsley & Robertson, 1996; W. M. Jones, 1997; Salas, Burke, & Cannon-Bowers, 2000). They also monitor their own performance and ask for help from their teammates or take other actions to compensate for deficiencies, such as taking a rest break or deferring tasks to others. They similarly attempt to have an understanding of how complete their own SA is (meta-SA) so that they can act to gather more information and delay decision making if needed and possible (Endsley, 2020; Endsley & Jones, 2012).

<u>SA of AI Teammate</u> - SA is critical for human oversight of any type of automation (Endsley, 2017b), and AI is no exception. Without good SA, people will be highly challenged in understanding what the AI is currently doing or will do. When the AI encounters situations that are not in its previous training, for example, it will fail to perform correctly, requiring the human to detect and overcome this deficiency, often with little time or advanced warning of the problem. In many high consequence systems where AI is being explored (e.g., driving, flying, military command and control, medical procedures), timely interventions by skilled humans are very important for overall team resilience and system safety. Therefore, human SA of AI performance is a cornerstone of HAT performance. Effective oversight of AI requires people to understand whether the AI is able to perform in its current situation (i.e., the sufficiency of its programming), the sufficiency of what it knows about (e. g., ability to accurately detect and incorporate relevant situational data), and the impact of the system’s actions on operational goals and others.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 4. Consistent SA on common goals is required for shared SA in teams.

Frequently SA of the AI has been thought of as part of system SA, supporting taskwork. For AI systems with limited teamwork capabilities this is probably sufficient. However, as AI systems become more highly capable and able to support more complex team behaviors, this designation becomes less clear since agent SA also becomes important for supporting more complex team behaviors.

<u>SA of Human Teammate</u> - There may also be an advantage to AI systems that have SA of the performance of their human teammate. For example, the automatic ground collision avoidance system (Auto-GCAS) provides automated take-over of aircraft flight control in order to recover to a safe attitude when it detects that the pilot is on a collision course with terrain (Ho et al., 2017). Other research is working to develop physiological sensors to detect pilot state (such as loss of consciousness or overload), that could be used to inform automated systems of the need to take control. (Lim, Ramasamy, Gardi, Kistan, & Sabatini, 2018; Liu, Gardi, Ramasamy, Lim, & Sabatini, 2016). While these systems may rely on more traditional forms of automation, by extension such capabilities can be envisioned for future AI systems. When AI systems become capable of monitoring the human teammate, and are able to provide teamwork behaviors such as dynamic anticipation of information needs, intervention and back-up, agent SA may also support teamwork activities.

<u>SA of Oneself</u> – People also need to maintain meta-awareness of their own ability to perform tasks, their effectiveness, and the sufficiency of their own SA. For example, when people are aware of the effects of fatigue, excessive workload, or insufficient training they may shift tasks to other team members in order to improve team performance (Dierdorff, Fisher, & Rubin, 2019; Dorneich et al., 2017; National Research Council, 1993).

Similarly, AI systems that have the ability to understand their own ability to perform properly in a situation would be better able to effectively transition tasks to human teammates in a timely manner (e.g., SAE Level 3 automated vehicles that provide human teammates with advanced warning of the need for human intervention). As the AI becomes capable of understanding its own SA state (including when it is poor), it can better communicate with the human, also improving teamwork.

## 3.3. Teamwork SA

Teamwork is defined as behaviors that support team member interactions, such as cooperation, communication, coordination, offering suggestions, acceptance of suggestions and adaptability (Baker & Salas, 1992). In effective teams, SA on the state of other team member’s goals, current functional assignments and decisions (including strategies and plans) are highly important for supporting these higher-level teamwork activities, and shared SA in HATs will similarly need to include these elements (Endsley, 2017b; U. S. Air Force, 2015). Teamwork SA needs include:

(a) Current goals – in order to align goals as priorities change;

(b) Current functional assignments – in order to ensure that all functions are being addressed as assignments are dynamically reallocated based on the relative capabilities and status of both the human and AI over time and across different types of situational demands;

(c) Current decisions, including strategies, plans, and actions – in order to support team coordination as the human and AI decide how to perform their various functions; and

(d) Task status – as an ongoing understanding of what actions have been taken by the other teammate and how successful those actions are at achieving shared goals is important for understanding when shifts in functional assignments are needed (e.g., stepping in to assist the other teammate), as well as for coordinating actions.

In the context of the earlier example in Table 2 for a HAT with an automated vehicle, teamwork SA requirements for managing a lane change are shown in Table 3.

Supporting these team SA needs can significantly enhance team performance. For instance, Miller and Hannen (1999) showed that by displaying the current goal of the AI system, pilots were able to easily detect and change its high-level goals to better align the AI’s goals with human goals (for example, landing versus go-around at an airport). Robots that can anticipate the information needs of their human counterparts and automatically provide that information have also been shown to improve team performance by reducing the time required for explicit team coordination (Chiou et al., 2021). These examples mimic the coordination that is seen in high performing human teams, for example a scrub nurse that projects the surgeon’s next tasks in order to provide the right instruments in advance of being asked for them.

Achieving these many different SA needs in HAT comes through a combination of team SA mechanisms, devices and processes.

## 4. Team SA mechanisms in HAT

Mental models are known to be important for understanding how systems operate in general (Johnson-Laird, 1980; Rouse & Morris, 1985). SA has been described as the current instantiation of the mental model (Endsley, 2000), representing the current status of relevant mental model elements, Fig. 5. For example, a mechanic would have a mental model of how a car engine works in general, and also might have SA about the current state of a particular car engine (e.g. it is at 2000 RPM, temperature is normal, and there is a knocking sound that indicates a carburetor problem). Relevant aspects of a system that would typically be included in a mental model include the system’s components, logic used, how it functions, its overall reliability, and its capabilities and limitations for performing different types of tasks. With respect to SA, a person might focus on how the system is currently performing, and how its capabilities and limitations will affect performance in the current context, as informed by these aspects of the mental model.

In relation to SA, mental models are important for (a) dynamically directing attention to relevant information, (b) developing an understanding of observed information, and (c) projecting the likely states of elements in the future (Endsley, 1995). The higher levels of SA (comprehension and projection) are highly dependent on having good mental models of the domain, actors, and systems within it. Mental

models provide a key mechanism that underpins people’s ability to integrate the large volumes of data that are present to form an understanding of what is happening and projecting system dynamics in a timely manner.

In addition to mental models of the task environment and other systems they operate, people need to develop effective mental models of the AI. Typically, mental models include an understanding of the logic used by the system and its capabilities and limitations (e.g., what is able to do or not do). These mental models may be formed by experience with the AI based on direct observation of its outputs and performance, or by training (e.g., history of the system, specific instruction on how it works, its errors and reliability). The person’s mental model of the AI is particularly important for being able to understand when it is acting correctly, and for being able to actively project when to rely on it, or when to take over control.

In teams of people, the presence of shared mental models (defined as a consistent understanding and representation of how systems work (components, content, structural relationships and cause and effect) help drive the rapid development of shared SA (Bolstad & Endsley, 1999; Endsley & Jones, 2001; Stout, Cannon-Bowers, & Salas, 1996). People with shared mental models (developed through common training and shared experiences) are more likely to arrive at consistent comprehension and projections of information without requiring a lot of detailed verbal communication (Mosier & Chidester, 1991).

Similarly, it is expected that shared mental models will be highly useful for supporting shared SA in HAT, however, this will be much more difficult than in human-human teams. First it is likely that AI will operate with very different processes and may operate on very different cues or sensor inputs than people (Liao, Gruen, & Miller, 2020; T. Miller, 2019). Further, the processes they use are generally quite opaque and constitute a “black-box” from the perspective of the human. In addition, because AI based on learning systems may change and update frequently, people will be considerably challenged to develop and maintain an accurate mental model of how the system works (Casner & Hutchins, 2019; Endsley, 2017a; U. S. Air Force, 2015).

Thus, developing a mental model of AI in HAT will be much harder and requires additional support. This will either necessitate extensive and ongoing training to develop a mental model of how the AI works (which would be logistically challenging), or increased attention to the development of explicit mechanisms for communicating information between the human and AI system in the form of Team SA devices.

## 5. Team SA devices for HAT

Teams rely on a number of devices for sharing information in order to update and align their views on what is happening. This can include direct communications (verbal or non-verbal), information obtained by existing in a common environment (e.g., shared observations of events), and/or reliance on shared displays that provide teammates with relevant and up-to-date situation information on the task, system and environment. In human-human teams, it has been shown that people make active trade-offs between different SA devices, relying more on one when others are not available (Bolstad & Endsley, 1999).

These same devices may be considered in relation to HAT. The ability for people to rely on forming shared SA with AI based on existing in a common environment is problematic. AI systems will rely on very different sets of sensors than people, and have different algorithms for processing and translating that sensory data. Therefore, there is a significant likelihood that they may arrive at a different understanding of the environment than the human teammate based solely on data collected by its sensors.

Currently methods for verbal and non-verbal communications between people and AI also remain quite limited. Research is being directed at developing natural language understanding (Sheth, Gaur, Roy, & Faldu, 2021), as well as non-verbal communications with AI, such as gesture recognition (Barattini, Morand, & Robertson, 2012; Liang, Proft, Andersen, & Knepper, 2019; Pavlovic, Colombo, Lim, & Casalegno, 2019) and emotion recognition (Pal, Mukhopadhyay, & Suryadevara, 2021) that may be pertinent in future, however, most communication is likely to occur through shared displays.

Given that people and AI systems may have limited verbal and non-verbal communication channels, and they may have very different sensors for gathering information directly from the environment, this means more emphasis will need to be placed on developing displays to create shared SA in HAT (U. S. Air Force, 2015). These displays (most likely visual or auditory) will provide the primary means of communicating between the AI and the human what the AI’s current understanding of the world is, as well as projections for the future, and the many factors relevant to teamwork SA, such as its plans, goals, and functional assignments. These displays will need to have the ability to not only communicate the AI’s situational model, but also to provide the human teammate with the ability to easily correct it when needed to better align world views and goals within the HAT.

Two key features of AI displays have received considerable research: the degree to which they provide explainability of AI actions and recommendations, and the development of AI displays with high levels of transparency. The overall goal of both is to provide people with needed insights into the system’s actions and behaviors in order to achieve operational objectives. While both methods provide significant value for improving team SA in HAT, both also have limitations and need considerable improvements for achieving these objectives, which will be explored in more depth.

System transparency is defined as “the understandability and pre-dictability of the system” (Endsley et al., 2003, p. 146). Chen et al. (2014, p. 2) define it as the system’s “abilities to afford an operator’s comprehension about an intelligent agent’s intent, performance, future plans, and reasoning process”. Display transparency refers to the real-time support for SA provided by the AI system through its interface. Display transparency is current and prospective, focused on what is happening now and in the near future.

Explainability also supports SA of AI systems, but it generally provides information in a retrospective manner, describing the logic, process, factors, or reasoning on which the system’s actions or recommendations were based. In this sense, explainability has traditionally focused on why the system did something (system capabilities or processes) whereas transparency focuses on what (relevant situational information). Therefore, while explainability is important for building an accurate mental model of the AI, in many time-constrained operations AI transparency will be more important for real-time SA. Since mental models are very important for SA, however, AI explainability indirectly supports SA.

## 5.1. Transparency

Wickens, Helton, Hollands and Banbury (2022) report significant benefits of system transparency for reducing the negative effects of out-of-the-loop performance induced by automation across 15 studies. A recent meta-analysis by van de Merwe, Mallam and Nazir (2022) similarly found significant benefits of transparency of intelligent agents for SA and performance across 17 studies. Display transparency has been shown to be valuable for:

a) Improving oversight of automation and performance (Bagheri & Jamieson, 2004; Bass, Baumgart, & Shepley, 2013; Bean, Rice, & Keller, 2011; Beck, Dzindolet, & Pierce, 2007; Dzindolet et al., 2002; Mercado et al., 2016; Oduor & Wiebe, 2008; Selkowitz, Lakhmani, & Chen, 2017; Seppelt & Lee, 2007; Stowers et al., 2017);

b) Improving SA (Boyce, Chen, Selkowitz, & Lakhmani, 2015; Chen et al., 2014; Schmitt, Roth, Barber, Chen, & Schulte, 2018; Selkowitz et al., 2017); and

c) Improving the calibration of trust (Dadashi, Stedmon, & Pridmore, 2013; Gao & Lee, 2006; Hoff & Bashir, 2015; Lee & See, 2004; Mercado et al., 2016; Panganiban, Matthews, & Long, 2020; Selkowitz et al., 2017; Seong & Bisantz, 2008; Stowers et al., 2017; Wang, Jamieson, & Hollands, 2009).

Different studies have manipulated different types of SA information in their studies of transparency, however, making it difficult to generalize from one study to the next regarding what type of transparency is needed. Although there is considerable agreement that AI systems will need to be transparent (J. Y. Chen & Barnes, 2015; Lyons & Havig, 2014; Shively et al., 2017; U. S. Air Force, 2015), the types of information that need to be made transparent is less consistent across authors (National Academies of Sciences Engineering and Medicine, 2021). Further, some research has shown that different people may place different priorities on the types of transparency information they most value (Vorm & Miller, 2020).

Chen and colleagues (J. Y. Chen & Barnes, 2015; J. Y. C. Chen et al., 2018) and Endsley (Endsley, 2017b; 2021b; Endsley & Jones, 2001; U. S. Air Force, 2015) emphasize transparency for shared information across SA levels 1, 2 and 3. Consistent with this approach, Mercado et al. (2016) systematically added SA transparency for Level 1 SA information, Level 2 SA information and Level 3 SA information, finding improvements in trust and performance with each addition, along with decreases in misuse of automation. Selkowitz and colleagues (Selkowitz et al., 2017; Selkowitz, Lakhmani, Larios, & Chen, 2016) found improvements in performance associated with transparency of Level 3 SA information. Seppelt and Lee (2007) demonstrated improved performance in overcoming adaptive cruise control failures in a driving task when Level 2 and 3 information (time headway, time to collision and range rate) were displayed to drivers. Trapsilawati et al. (2017) found significant improvements in the performance of air traffic controllers when provided with both a conflict resolution aid and improved SA via a vertical situation display (VSD) where the SA information on the VSD helped to compensate for the imperfect aid. These studies reinforce a wide-body of research showing improvements in SA and performance associated with the display of relevant situation information (Endsley, 2021c).

Other authors have been more focused on the transparency of information about the automation agent itself, including its current state, what it is doing, how or reasons, errors and future behaviors (Sarter & Woods, 1995; Wickens, Helton, Hollands, & Banbury, 2022). The display of uncertainty (or confidence) information associated with system assessments have also been explored. Research has shown that displaying information on the reliability of sensors (such as through luminance levels) affects people’s reliance on that information (Montgomery & Sorkin, 1996). Stower’s et al. (2017) showed improved performance when the system’s confidence in its assessments was displayed to users. However, the way in which uncertainty information is pre-sented (e.g., graphically vs numerically, framing, modality) can have significant effects on how such information is used (Banbury, Selcon, Endsley, Gorton, & Tatlock, 1998; Basapur, Bisantz, & Kesavadas, 2003; Bisantz, Marsiglio, & Munch, 2005; McDermott et al., 2003). Further when confidence levels for different AI options are close, decision making time can increase significantly (Selcon, 1990).

Researchers have also focused on the value of making automation reliability information transparent during task performance. Bagheri and Jamieson (2004) showed that providing people with information on automation reliability allowed them to compensate for poorer automation reliability through improved attention strategies, improving their performance with low reliability systems. Bean et al. (2011) and Dzindolet et al. (2002) similarly found a performance advantage from pre-senting automation reliability information. Loft et al. (2021) found that information on a decision aid’s reliability led to a decrease in “checking behavior” for higher reliability aids, thus reducing workload and overall decision time. Beck et al. (2007) showed that in addition to providing information on automation reliability, training sessions were important for improving people’s willingness to accept accurate system advice.

Some authors also discuss transparency for teamwork SA needs. Endsley (2017b; U. S. Air Force, 2015) focuses on sharing information on goals, priorities, function allocation, plans and tasks, relative capabilities, impact on others and projected strategies actions and plans. In addition to goals and tasks, Lyons (2014) emphasizes the need for sharing of intent information as well as division of labor in the team (i.e., function allocation). Chen and colleagues (2014) also discuss the importance of making transparent the teammate’s roles and responsibilities, goals, projections and reasoning, as well as their contributions to shared tasks. Less research has been done exploring these aspects of AI transparency however.

As a means of unifying this work, it is stipulated that the SA requirements in Table 1 provide a way of framing the SA needs that should or could be transmitted via display transparency. That is, for AI to be transparent, SA information pertinent to the taskwork (i.e., Level 1, 2 and 3 SA) as well as information on the state of the AI (i.e., agent SA) are both important. In order for the AI to operate as a teammate, with teamwork behaviors, information supporting teamwork SA will also be relevant, and there may be more need for two-way sharing of SA between people and AI. Additional information that is sometimes discussed in terms of transparency (such as system logic or reasoning, history, capabilities and limitations, etc..) contributes more to the mental model of the system, indirectly supporting SA. This information is usually transmitted via explainability facilities rather than as a part of real-time transparency.

## 5.2. Explainability

In traditional AI systems, explainability was provided by the “why” feature that generated a list of rules associated with some recommendation (Scott, Clancey, Davis, & Shortliffe, 1977; Swartout, 1985). Since learning-based AI systems do not have overt rules that are encoded, developing improved explainability has been a key research focus for providing insight into what is happening within the black-box (Doran, Schulz, & Besold, 2017; Hagras, 2018). Early approaches to AI explainability included efforts to derive rules out of neural network systems as means of conveying system logic (Huang & Endsley, 1997).

More recent work on explainable AI creates written descriptions or displays that show which aspects of images are being used by the AI in making a classification (Goebel et al., 2018). While this information may be useful, it probably does not fully meet a user’s needs for operating with AI. People will still be required to slowly build up an understanding of the AI over time to determine its reliability or unreliability for appropriately classifying different types of objects. That is, they have to manually generate their own mental models of the system’s capabilities based on the presentation of level 1 SA (which information the system uses) across many cases. Since people can vary significantly in terms of how they might interpret such displays, this could lead to very different mental models from the same examples.

A number of problems with current approaches to AI explainability have been found (Druce, Niehaus, Moody, Jensen, & Littman, 2021). This research shows that a) explanations needed to be tailored to the specifics of the scenarios and situational circumstances in which the behavior occurred, b) many AI systems are very brittle and their logic is not easily amenable to explanation, c) methods for providing causal explanations of AI behavior are not straightforward, and d) people are prone to adopt highly inaccurate mental models of how AI systems work and these models are highly resistant to correction.

Doran, Schulz and Besold (2017) make the point that effective explanation systems need to create a line of reasoning that explains the AI behavior. Miller (2019) provides a detailed account of the social psychology literature surrounding what people expect from explanations. From the standpoint of human-AI interaction, people are primarily looking for answers as to why a system did something or made a particular decision as opposed to some other decision. That is, explanations should generally be both causative and contextual, providing a contrast as to why it did A vs B. This helps to build up an understanding of how the system functions in ways that will be applicable to future situations. It is important to note that effective explanations are generally not statistical representations, or schematic diagrams of system logic or architecture, but rather operationally relevant descriptions of how the system will perform in different circumstances. The goal for explainability is to augment the mental model developed during training and direct experience in order to allow the user to understand the system’s reliability for specific tasks and conditions, and to establish pre-dictability for system behavior.

A number of studies have found improved team performance from providing AI explanations. Zhou and Chen (2015) showed increased use of the system resulted from providing AI algorithms. Oduor and Wiebe (2008), showed improvements in system usage when the algorithm used by a decision aid was provided to users, improving both trust and performance. Bass et al. (2013) found that providing information about the strategy used by the automation as well as information about the environmental cues used by the system (Level 1 SA) provided a performance advantage for decision making in an air traffic control task, but the strategy information alone was not helpful unless the Level 1 SA information used by the system was also provided.

Paleja et al. (2021) investigated the use of text-based explanations and decision trees with AI of a robot performing a collaborative task with a human. They found significant improvements in both level 1 and level 2 SA from the AI explanations, however this translated into performance benefits only for novices, while it slowed down the experts due to overload. Shin (2021) found that AI explainability was associated with 58% of the variance of trust, with causability (causal understanding within a specified context) playing a significant role.

There is a clear need to develop an understanding of the capabilities and limitations of AI so people know in advance when it will be trustworthy, and when it won’t, in terms of the types of situations or conditions it can address. This allows them the ability to adopt effective strategies for using the AI and relying on its outputs, or taking on the task manually when needed. Approaches for explainable AI need to address this requirement directly. Along these lines, Sanneman and Shah (2022) have proposed an SA framework for explainable AI that recommends techniques for addressing SA at each of the three levels of SA, mapped to a delineation of SA requirements.

In addition, people need to be able to understand what the AI is doing within the context of the current situation. If the system is acting in a confusing or inappropriate manner, it needs to be transparent what the system’s inputs are (i.e., is it consistent with the human’s SA) and what its interpretations are (Level 2 and 3 SA), as well as its logic structures. When people are able to make these direct comparisons, they can learn more about how the system works and adopt appropriate workarounds when insufficient. This is reliant on real-time display transparency.

## 5.3. AI learning systems

A major challenge for human interaction with AI is the fact that AI based on learning systems can change in its capabilities dynamically over time in ways that may not be obvious. For example, an autonomous vehicle can learn to handle conditions it could not previously (e.g., lane merges or sharp corners), or could fail to perform in other conditions where it previously had been successful (e.g., due to the use of a different sensor suite or changes to algorithms). These changes might be invisible to the user (and perhaps even the developers). While there is certainly a need for ongoing training with learning-based AI systems, it also will be important to make agent SA and capabilities more transparent in realtime to help compensate for the likelihood of out-of-date mental models (Endsley, 2017b; U. S. Air Force, 2015).

Miller (2021) makes the case that pre-operational training (including planning or mission rehearsal sessions) or post-operational debriefing sessions will be critical for building up expectations of system behavior through AI explainability because people won’t have time to absorb this information in demanding real-time operations. That is, explainability of AI in low workload periods before or after working with the system will be critical due to information overload during real-time operations. This may also be the case. A significant challenge exists in creating effective displays for transparently conveying the information that is critical for SA in ways that do not induce overload. Whether this will require improved display transparency, new forms of explainability, better training, or a combination of all three remains to be determined.

## 5.4. Limits of transparency and explainability

Although AI transparency and explainability are important for human interaction with AI, they are not in themselves sufficient for good SA. In addition, it is important that needed information be salient and integrated to be effective (Endsley & Jones, 2012).

In many, if not most, jobs, people need to deal with a significant amount of information overload. It is quite easy for important information to get lost in busy displays with a lot of competing information. When AI is performing parts of job, the negative effects of low vigilance are a problem; people’s attention may easily wander to other competing tasks. For example, SA errors were found to occur in 30% of cases in a study of pilots and air traffic controllers when all of the needed information was present on the display, but people were distracted with other tasks and information (D. G. Jones & Endsley, 1996). Unless the AI presents relevant information in a manner that is salient (highly distinguishable from the background noise visually or auditorily), people may still fail to understand what the AI is doing.

Secondly, information integration is important. If relevant AI information is not integrated with other related task information, the likelihood it will be observed decreases in time-demanding situations, making it less transparent. To be accessible and useable, relevant information needs to be integrated around key decisions and goals. This reduces the time to find relevant information as well as decreases the potential for missing relevant information.

Finally, the idea of meaningful control (Boardman & Butcher, 2019) is pertinent. Good AI transparency will be insufficient if the human cannot act on that information in a timely manner. This includes several considerations.

1. The human needs to have sufficient SA to be able detect and understand what the AI is doing (i.e., alert and engaged in the operational task and not out-of-loop, as well as provided with the relevant information).

2. People need to be able to intervene in a timely manner. When people are actively engaged in the control loop, this means the time required to detect a problem, decide on a solution and execute the appropriate maneuver $( \mathsf { t _ { d e t e c t } } + \mathsf { t _ { d e c i d e } } + \mathsf { t _ { e x e c u t e } } )$ . When overseeing $\mathbf { A } ,$ however, they also incur additional time required to determine that the AI is unable to act appropriately in that situation $\mathbf { ( \mathfrak { t } _ { \mathsf { d e t e c t } }   +   \mathfrak { t } _ { \mathsf { d e c i d e } }   +   \mathfrak { t } }$ override + t<sub>execute</sub>). Thus, a one-step decision turns into a two-step decision (Endsley, 2017a), which may be subject to automation inertia – the tendency to stay in an automated mode, not recognizing that override is called for.

3. People need to have the control functionality required to execute an appropriate solution. In cases where interventions are difficult, or people have not been trained on appropriate responses, the time to execute may increase and the ability to execute a response can be significantly reduced, such as was the case with accidents on the Boeing 737-Max 8 (Endsley, 2019).

## 5.5. Improving SA and transparency in Human-AI teams

Methods for supporting SA through display transparency in human-AI teams and the types of information included have been inconsistent across studies. A systematic method for determining which aspects of SA need to be provided in the displays for a given AI application needs to be applied in transparency research, and effective methods for achieving transparency, within the confines of workload and temporal task demands, are needed (National Academies of Sciences Engineering and Medicine, 2021). These needs can be addressed through SA Oriented Design (SAOD) (Endsley et al., 2003; Endsley & Jones, 2012).

The goal of transparency is to enable “the operator to maintain proper SA of the system in its tasking environment without becoming overloaded” (Mercado et al., 2016, p. 402). Automation transparency is a key principle of SAOD which was developed to create system displays to support SA and decision making in highly complex domains where information overload and noisy data are common. It specifically deals with the challenges of maintaining SA with automation and AI through detailed design principles. Importantly, it provides a systematic approach for determining what SA information needs to be displayed for a given application, and how to go about creating transparent displays to support SA in that context.

SAOD involves three main phases: SA requirements analysis, iterative design of the user interface using SA design principles, and evaluation of user interface displays using SA metrics in addition to performance and workload assessments. This process can be applied to the development of transparent displays for supporting human-AI team operations.

<u>SA Requirements</u> – In the first phase, a GDTA is conducted for the relevant domain and role to determine the goals, decisions and SA requirements (at all three levels) needed to make each decision. Details for conducting a GDTA can be found in Endsley (2021b) and Endsley and Jones (2012). The GDTA specifies the information needed for the entire job, including both routine and non-routine situations. In the GDTA, no decisions have been made about what functions might be automated or what functions the AI might assume. The focus is primarily on determining which information is needed to make a decision, not on how it will be obtained (which can vary across system designs, individuals and situations). The GDTA not only provides a comprehensive list of information needs, but also much needed guidance on which information needs to be used together, as well as how information needs to be processed to arrive at comprehension and projection. These aspects are unique to the GDTA and are not typically found in other design approaches. These SA requirements correspond to the taskwork elements of team SA in Table 1.

<u>SA Design</u> – In the second phase, rapid prototyping is used to create system designs that provide the information identified in the GDTA based on 50 SAOD principles. These principles were developed based on a cognitive model of SA and research on SA in a wide variety of domain areas. The SAOD principles translate that research into easy to apply rules for effective system designs that will support high levels of SA at manageable workload levels. Specifically, these rules work to support processes that people rely on for good SA (e.g., pattern recognition, multi-tasking), while helping to reduce the negative effects of common SA problems (e.g., attentional narrowing, out-of-the-loop problems due to automation, working memory limitations).

In addition to general design principles, SAOD includes principles focused on alarms, coping with complexity, display of confidence (uncertainty) information, automation, and supporting team SA. A subset of the SAOD principles is shown in Table 4, relevant to the task of creating transparent displays for AI. Whereas typical human factors design guidelines focus on human perception or physical requirements, SOAD provides the added advantage of supporting human cognition and understanding of information.

These design principles are important for supporting SA of the overall job to be conducted by the human. The goal of making the portions of the job that the AI is doing transparent must be considered within the context of the other tasks and information that the individual is conducting. That is, it would be short-sighted to create a system that makes the AI’s operations clear, if that is only one portion of the overall job of the individual. The ability of the person to have the SA required to oversee the AI within the context of other tasks being conducted is important.

<u>SA Measurement</u> – The final phase of the SAOD process is the evaluation of the interface to determine how well it achieves the objectives of high operator SA, manageable workload and effective performance in both normal and abnormal conditions. Objective measures of SA are used to identify whether display designs are effective in supporting SA requirements, and to identify potential SA problems that may exist (Endsley, 2021b). An iterative process is then used to refine the system displays to address any shortcomings.

Table 4

SA-oriented design principles related to display transparency for HAT.

| Section | Principles |
| --- | --- |
| General Principles | Organize information around goalsPresent Level 2 information directly—support comprehensionProvide assistance for Level 3 SA projectionsMake critical cues for schema activation salientSupport transmission of different comprehensions and projections across teams |
| Complexity Principles | Minimize logic branchesMap system functions to the goals and mental models of usersProvide system transparency and observabilityGroup information based on Level 2/3 SA requirements and goalsReduce display density, but don’t sacrifice coherence |
| Automation Principles | Use automation for assistance in carrying out routine actions rather than higher level cognitive tasksProvide SA support rather than decisionsKeep the operator in control and in the loopAvoid the proliferation of automation modesMake modes and system states salientEnforce automation consistencyAvoid advanced queuing of tasksAvoid the use of information cueingUse methods of decision support that create human/system symbiosisProvide automation transparency |
| Uncertainty Principles | Support sensor reliability assessmentExplicitly identify missing informationSupport assessment of confidence in composite data |
| Alarm Management Principles | Don’t make people rely on alarms—provide projection supportSupport alarm confirmation activitiesSupport the rapid development of global SA of systems in an alarm state |

## 5.6. Example: transparent displays for autonomous driving

As an example, SAOD will be applied to the challenge of creating transparent displays to support the SA of a human involved in driving with an AI that can assume the functionality for managing vehicle speed and trajectory (i.e., semi-autonomous driving). For this example, the display design for the Tesla autopilot will be considered. Based on a GDTA for the driving domain (Endsley, 2021b), Table 5 shows the SA requirements for the goals “maintain desired lane and speed” and “avoid other vehicles”. (SA requirements associated with other goals are not shown here for brevity.)

If this function were being performed manually, the driver would be constantly monitoring vehicle position and trajectory to detect or project deviations that require steering or speed corrections. If the function is assigned to the autopilot, then the vehicle automation (controlled by AI in this case) monitors this same information and automatically makes the needed corrections to maintain the desired speed and lane as set by the driver. The driver, however, also would need to monitor the autopilot’s performance in order to take over control, and therefore would need access to the same information. The driver also has new SA requirements associated with the AI agent: (a) automation state/mode, (b) ability to perform tasks (reliability), (c) status and performance, (d) projected actions, (e) impact on others, and (f) SA sufficiencyas shown in Table 1.

The effectiveness of Tesla’s autopilot and displays for supporting SA have previously been reported in Endsley (2017a). Fig. 6 shows the current situation display that supports autopilot and adaptive cruise control (ACC) operations. Although the Tesla autopilot has a number of display features that support SA, that study found a number of shortcomings associated with the transparency of the autopilot.

<u>Taskwork SA</u> - While certain relevant Level 1 SA information is displayed effectively (e.g., vehicle position in lane, selected lane, other vehicles detected, current speed, speed limits and selected speed), other information is missing. In particular, vehicles in the blind spot are not shown. Further, with current sensor suites that rely on cameras rather than radar, vehicles that are shown may be inaccurate in their position by as much as one-half to a full car length, depending on relative speeds, or can move around, providing visual “jitter” that is distracting to drivers. Most Level 2 and Level 3 SA information is not directly pre-sented but rather has to be visually assessed and mentally computed by the driver (e.g., distance to another vehicle, lane deviations, projected deviations in speed or lane keeping).

| Location of nearby objects(vehicles, pedestrians,cyclists, other objects) | Compliance withplanned route | Projected distance to turnsor highway exits |
| Speed and heading of nearbyobjects (vehicles,pedestrians, cyclists) | Deviation fromdesired speed | Projected traffic stops andslowdowns ahead |
| Relative speed andacceleration of traffic inadjacent lanes | Deviation from lanelimits | Projected deviation fromspeed |
| Open areas in adjacent lanes | Distance to otherobjects, vehicles,pedestrians, cyclists | Projected deviation fromlane |
| Speed limit |  | Projected change in speedand direction of vehicle(s) |
| Stop light status |  |  |
| Lane markings |  |  |
| Traffic control measures |  |  |

<u>Agent SA</u> - The autopilot provides some information on the state of the AI, namely whether it is on or off and its current setting (i.e., selected lane and speed). A critical issue is that while the Tesla displays provide good information on the mode of the system (though blue symbols that show each system is activated), it is very poor at making changes in modes salient to the driver. An auditory tone provided when the autopilot disconnects is very low and hard to hear over typical road noise or the radio (i.e., it is not salient), thus transparency is not very high, decreasing awareness of automatic or accidental autopilot disconnects.

The autopilot can only be activated in conjunction with the ACC. Unfortunately, the two systems interact in unintuitive ways (i.e., emergent behaviors), making the vehicle prone to unexpected speed surges when changing lanes or leaving an area with a median, for example. The logic used by the system is not provided to drivers either in manuals or through training, and it can change as frequently as once per month via internet updates. Explainability of the AI is not provided; thus, it is very difficult to maintain an accurate mental model of how the automation performs, making system understandability and predictability low in many cases.

Further no information is provided on system confidence levels. Depictions of other vehicles can change from sedans to trucks to motorcycles, and might switch back and forth between them, lowering confidence in system capabilities. Tesla’s decision to switch to camera only assessments of environmental information (as opposed to using radar or lidar), and its subsequent effect on reliability of objects, was not conveyed to drivers. No information is provided on the sufficiency of its situation information that drivers could use to adjust their expectations or behaviors.

The system’s ability to perform in the current context is missing. It does not convey temporal information regarding system actions and limitations (e.g., ability to perform in upcoming conditions, future trajectories). Even though autopilot shortcomings are rare in good highway conditions, they can happen under certain circumstances (e.g., lane merges, lane splits, sharp curves, stop lights, closure on vehicles at high rates of speed, lane changes). Autopilot failures are also very frequent on surface streets (where lane markings are not present) which, in practice, prevents its usage in those conditions. However, these problems can only be surmised by the driver over time though experience. No training or instructions detailing the systems’ capabilities and limitations are provided to drivers.

<u>Teamwork SA</u> - Although it is fairly easy to determine that the autopilot is engaged and what it is currently doing, an inability to project its actions makes automation surprise a problem. Information on its goals and plans is largely absent.

Fig. 7 shows recommendations for display changes that would supply improved transparency for the Tesla autopilot, following SAOD principles. Fig. 7(a) shows needed improvements to AI transparency through the display of vehicles in the blind spot (Show Level 1 SA organized around goals), alerts for potential lane incursions (Provide assistance for Level 3 SA projections), violations of speed limits (Present Level 2 SA information directly), and changes in speed (Show Level 1 SA organized around goals). In this example, not only is the driver able to better predict the future dynamics of their own and other vehicles, but the implications of that information for potential actions (e.g., swerving into the adjacent lane) are clear. Further the vehicle’s current actions (slowing even though the vehicle is below its set speed) are more transparent (Provide system transparency and observability). In cases where the reasons for its actions are not obvious, this would help significantly.

Fig. 7(b) shows a display to provide improved predictability of the AI’s intended path (Provide automation transparency). An occasional problem occurs at highway off-ramps when the AI tracks the lane markings on the right rather than the left of the lane, leading it to try to exit the highway inappropriately. This “surprise” event can cause the driver to need to swerve to gain control and stay on the highway. Furthermore, the vehicle often unexpectedly speeds up on exit ramps. This occurs because the pacing vehicle in front is no longer there, causing the vehicle to speed up to its set speed based on the ACC, even though people normally want to slow down on a highway exit ramp. By clearly displaying the vehicle’s projected pathway, and any changes in speed that will occur, the improved transparency can be used by drivers to override the AI in a timely manner, and minimize automation surprise.
