Fig. 7. Examples of improvements in AI transparency for Tesla autopilot.

Fig. 7(c) and (d) show displays to improve transparency at lane merges. The Tesla AI currently does not handle lane merges well. It can lose its ability to hold to a straight path (wandering within the wider area at the merge point), which can be disconcerting when not expected. Furthermore, it is not able to detect adjacent vehicles and adjust its speed to carry out a safe merge. In these cases, the driver is responsible for detecting any issues and correcting for them. Fig. 7(c) displays a salient shaded area as a warning that the vehicle is approaching an area where it might be unreliable (e.g., lane merges, lane splits, sharp curves, stop lights), along with a description of the potential problem (Support reliability assessments). Fig. 7(d) increases the warning level and shows conflicting vehicle trajectories entering the area (Provide assistance for Level 3 projections). These examples of display transparency focus on embedded contextual cues relevant to system capabilities and limitations and their impact on system behaviors in the near future.

While it would be best if the AI were robust enough to handle these types of situations, these examples show how transparently presented, meaningful, salient and contextually embedded information can be used to boost driver performance in working with even imperfect AI. In particular the displays focus on relevant comprehension and projection information needed to align the driver’s and AI’s situation assessments (perceptions, understanding and projections of objects in the environment). The AI’s ability to perform within the context of the current situation is made clear, along with its current and projected actions and impact on others. In this sense, the improved display transparency goes beyond mere training or explainability of the AI in an abstract sense, to provide actionable information on its behavior in the current situation. This will be particularly important in situations where through learning or changes in sensor capabilities, the AI’s behavior may change in unanticipated or confusing ways.

In addition, improving the salience of the current mode (e.g., through a louder and more salient auditory tone) would be very helpful in improving the transparency of autopilot operations (Make modes and system states salient), making it less likely that drivers would be unaware of an automatic or inadvertent mode change. Another key improvement would be better integrating the autopilot displays with the out-the-window view (Organize information around goals). Currently attention to autopilot displays requires considerable time looking away from the current driving situation, where critical information the vehicle may not be aware of, such as debris in the road or the presence of an unseen vehicle or pedestrian, would appear. In the future, the use of a head-up display (HUD) for projecting relevant display information georeferenced over relevant real-world information (i.e., augmented reality) should be explored as a potential means for improving driver SA.

These examples address transparency for taskwork SA and agent SA. As automated vehicles become more capable, they could potentially be able to support more team-like behaviors. This could include more intelligent routing and re-routing of the vehicle on the basis of a better understanding of the goals and priorities of the driver. Currently, most auto-routing systems provide between one and three recommended routes based on the shortest distance to the indicated destination and a limited consideration of road types. However, people do not just optimize time on route, they also tend to be risk-adverse, taking into account factors such as the complexity of the route (number of turns or highway changes), the likelihood the route will take the vehicle through a traffic prone area (such as downtown at rush hour, or roads known by the driver to have high traffic volumes), and other safety considerations (such as not making left hand turns). At other times drivers may prioritize other factors such as speed, scenery, or the availability of restaurants. A system that can better understand driver goals and priorities would be able to recommend and execute routes in ways that show better coordination with the driver.

Conversely, displays that allow drivers to see and adjust AI goals and priorities would similarly provide better teaming. An advanced AI that could anticipate driver needs (e.g., the need for a rest-break, recommendations for good places to eat or sleep on long trips, the best place to recharge) would exhibit better teamwork behaviors. Doing so effectively (rather than being a nuisance) requires that the AI understand driver goals and plans. Better shared SA between the two agents is necessary to support these types of teaming behaviors.

## 6. Team SA processes

Effective human-human teams also form good processes for sharing and comparing information to help maintain a consistent understanding of the situation. For example, effective teams engage in contingency planning to develop shared mental models for emergencies, have democratic leaders who encourage and model information sharing, and ensure the team is on the same page before preceding to problem resolution (Orasanu & Salas, 1993). They also have a group norm of information sharing and cross checking with each other, as well as prioritizing goals and imagining possible future events so that contingency plans can be established (Taylor, Endsley, & Henderson, 1996). Poor teams on the other hand have been found to be overly reliant on expectations, and easily distracted by unexpected problems. Information sharing is not the norm and team SA can be easily misdirected by team members with a strong personality.

Little has been done to determine what effective team processes for HAT might consist of, however, and it has been noted there needs to be a better understanding of the types of team processes that will be effective for HAT (Demir, Cooke, & Amazeen, 2018; McNeese et al., 2018; National Academies of Sciences Engineering and Medicine, 2021). If AI systems can be designed to be more transparent and more explainable (or at least understandable) by human teammates, will this be sufficient for supporting the types of team processes (e.g., coordination) that are needed? Or will additional strategies and techniques for information sharing in HAT be needed?

One approach would be to attempt to duplicate effective humanhuman team processes. AI systems could potentially be trained to call human attention to critical information and encourage projection and contingency planning for example. The need for AI systems to better anticipate and support human information needs proactively has been identified (O’Neill et al., 2020).

AI systems also might be trained to help detect and compensate for poor SA in human teammates. Processes for assessing people’s SA through physiological sensors are being developed that could potentially be used to detect low SA states (e.g., loss of vigilance, overload, surprise) which could theoretically provide AI systems with needed insights into SA deficiencies (Bailey, Scerbo, Freeman, Mikulka, & Scott, 2003; Bracken, Tobyne, Winder, Shamsi, & Endsley, 2021; Zhang et al., 2020). Upon detecting a low SA state, the AI could then provide appropriate interventions such as off-loading tasks or recommending breaks.

Approaches such as these will require very careful development and testing to ensure that they are successful and do not introduce unwanted interruptions in task performance. The development of adaptive automation is notoriously difficult, with interventions (such as Microsoft’s Clippy™) being more likely to be annoying than helpful. Similarly, AI systems that attempt to automatically determine human tasks, priorities, and needs can easily be incorrect and can inadvertently undermine team performance instead (Calhoun, 2021; Kaber, Riley, Tan, & Endsley, 2001; C. A. Miller, Funk, Goldman, Meisner, & Wu, 2005). In that AI systems are different than people in many ways, it is likely that significant new research is needed to determine effective team processes for HAT.

## 7. Conclusions

AI display transparency and explainability each have unique roles for supporting the SA and mental models of people who need to interact with and oversee AI operations. These facets of system development are crucial to achieving both appropriate levels of trust and team performance when working with AI systems. Future research is needed to design effective AI transparency techniques and to demonstrate that needed SA and trust at manageable workload levels are achieved in the real-world conditions where these systems will be used. The temporal demands of the situation (time available for reviewing information, making decisions and carrying out actions) will have a significant impact on the approaches that may be feasible. In that future projections in many domains often involve not only extrapolations of current trends, but also a consideration of possible or likely future actions of others, methods to assist people with envisioned worlds are also needed.

Methods for resolving conflicts in SA between human and AI systems will also be needed. In a given situation it is possible that the AI may have better SA than the human, or that the human may know more than the AI. Effective methods for determining when people should accept the AI’s picture of the situation versus when they should over-ride it, and easy methods for correcting SA across the two agents, need to be determined. In addition to considerations of transparency and explainability, more research is also needed to develop AI approaches that will overcome or reduce the SA deficits that are common to automation of various types. It will be important to explore different role structures for people and AI that may provide advantages to team performance without encountering OOTL disadvantages.

AI is still in its infancy in delivering on promises of “intelligence”. Fulfillment of this goal is dependent on equipping AI with better sensors and capabilities for gathering SA of the world it is operating in, and for transforming that information into relevant representations for decision making that are reliable and robust. In addition, it will require improved capabilities for working with people — making its behaviors understandable and predictable, as well as supporting higher level teamwork behaviors.
